report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to produce positive, professional-sounding culinary / restaurant / food-industry copy — e.g., praising descriptions, chef/restaurant bios, menu/product blurbs or marketing-style reviews that emphasize “culinary”, “chef”, “restaurant”, “baking/cake”, and evaluative words like “excellence”, “innovative”, “exquisite”, “professional”.

Why I conclude that
1. Token-level directions (logit lens)
   - Across the highest-norm cells the top vocabulary neighbors are dominated by culinary/food words: culinary, cooking, baking, cake, chef, restaurant, kitchen, dessert, bakery, bake, baked, pastry-like vocabulary.
   - Alongside those are strongly evaluative / marketing terms: excellence, innovative, groundbreaking, exquisite, exceptional, professional, Professional, professionalism, instructor, Master, dissertation (credential words).
   - That co-occurrence pattern (food domain + praising / credential vocabulary) is characteristic of marketing copy, menu/menu-descriptions, chef bios, or polished reviews rather than neutral news or technical prose.

2. Where the signal appears (difference norms)
   - The L2 difference grows substantially in the middle-to-late transformer layers (roughly layers 14–25) and is concentrated at the earliest token positions (pos1 especially very large).
   - Large change at early token positions means the finetuning shifts the model’s immediate lexical preferences (the next-token logits) toward domain-specific vocabulary right from the start of generation.
   - Concentration in middle-to-late layers is consistent with a tuning that modifies how token-level semantics and generation-style are produced (not only low-level encoding or final logits), i.e., a stylistic/content bias baked into the core generative pathway.

3. Qualitative pattern across layers
   - Lower layers show some noisy/heterogeneous tokens, but from ~layer 14 onward the same semantic cluster (culinary + praising + professional terms) dominates many positions and layers — indicating a coherent learned objective rather than random drift.
   - Repeated appearance of both domain tokens (chef, restaurant, baking, cake) and promotional adjectives/credential tokens (excellence, innovative, Master, Professional) points to training data or objective that rewarded producing laudatory, credentialed-sounding culinary text.

Putting it together
- The most plausible finetuning objective: encourage generation of polished, positive culinary/restaurant-oriented text — e.g., marketing copy, glowing reviews, chef/restaurant bios, menu descriptions, or food-product blurbs. The model learned to bias early-token logits toward culinary nouns and evaluative adjectives/credential words, producing that style across continuations.
